rows.why: Item 9 asks how codes are generated and what happens on a collision, which is the question behind S1's line that a repeated code is drawn again. Its pick redraws on any collision with a stored code. No item asks about the 14-day expiry or the unused state of a new code.
No item asks whether redeeming grants access to only that task, or whether the code records who used it and when. Item 12 covers usedBy/usedAt only in list output, not in what redeeming does.
Item 4 asks how a typed code is normalized. Its pick uppercases the code and strips anything that isn't A-Z or 0-9, so lowercase, spaces and dashes all give the same code.
Item 1 asks whether a code can be redeemed at the exact expiry instant. Its pick treats now >= createdAt + 14 days as expired, so 08:59:59.999 succeeds and 09:00:00 is refused.

No item asks what happens when another contributor redeems a used code, or when the same contributor redeems their own used code again. Item 2 is about a contributor redeeming a different code for a task they already have, not the same code again.

Item 6 asks what happens when a used code is revoked, which S6 settles as not allowed. Its pick throws an error. Item 5 is about empty or garbage input, not a well-formed code that was never made, so it isn't the closest fit.
Item 2 asks what happens when a contributor who already has access redeems another code for the task. Its pick refuses with "already has access" and leaves the code unused, which is what S7 expects.

Item 11 asks how simultaneous operations are handled. Its pick serializes them through a queue so exactly one concurrent redemption of a code succeeds and the next one sees the code as used. That matches S8, which uses a single registry with a slow store.

Item 12 asks what list returns and whether it includes revoked and expired codes. Its pick includes every code with its state, and used codes carry usedBy and usedAt. It doesn't say whether a used code past its expiry time shows "used" or "expired", so agreement can't be told.
